title: Regression: Shooting, Steals and Blocks
brief: Which shooting and defensive numbers from last season should we expect to move back toward normal, and how do we spot them before paying for them? It must cover regressing FT%, 3P% and 2P% outliers, steal and block conversion rates, and how three-point swings drive in-season buy-low and sell-high calls.
summary: Last season's shooting percentages and steal totals are the least reliable numbers you will see before the 2026-10-18 auction. Bid on attempts, rim contests and deflections, and assume extreme FT%, 3P%, 2P% and steal or block conversion rates drift back toward the player's norm. In season, three-point swings drive most buy-low and sell-high trades, so buy cold shooters and sell hot ones before the 2027-03-04 deadline.

paragraphs.text: Volume repeats from year to year. Accuracy does not. Three-point attempts per game correlate at 0.88 from one season to the next, and threes made at 0.86. Three-point percentage correlates at only 0.45. Two-point percentage is 0.53, true shooting 0.52 and free throw percentage 0.49.
Free throw percentage is now the least stable of our nine categories. It shares that label with steals as the most variable category year to year. FG% and three-point shooting also vary a lot.

Shooting reaches more than its own category. Three-point percentage is a hidden category: it moves 3PTM, PTS and FG%. FG% and FT% each touch two categories. In our 9-cat league, one shooting regression can cost you three weekly matchups at once.

So regress every shooting percentage in your projections before you set a bid. Players whose value depends on elite shooting carry the most risk. Treat any shooting improvement as a bonus, not a reason to pay more.

sections.heading: Spotting shooting outliers before the auction

paragraphs.text: Free throws: an unexpected swing in either direction usually does not last. It drifts back toward the player's norm, and you cannot predict it. Several players had big FT% drops last season with no clear reason, and that pattern likely reverts. On draft day, a player whose FT% fell sharply can be a quiet value. A player whose FT% jumped well above his career level should be priced on his career rate.
Do not call anyone a bad shooter as a fixed fact. Say how he shot last season. Only extreme cases like Giannis at the free throw line are close to certain.

Threes: a big jump in 3P% on the same volume should not be expected to repeat. A good 3P% on low volume does not make a reliable shooter either. Look for about five or six attempts per game, or a high share of shots from three. Be skeptical when a non-shooter rebuilds his jumper. One expert thinks it fails more often than it works.

Twos and FG%: if a 2P% starts with a 7, expect it to come down. Be wary of 70% field goal shooters in general, and of very high percentages on both twos and threes. A player with an outlier FG% can lose most of his edge from a small drop. Rim finishing is higher volume and more predictable than mid-range, but swings there matter more. An 11-point drop at the rim costs about 3 points of overall FG%. Also check who passes to him. Teammates who create shots, like elite passers, can push a player's finishing up or down.

Late spikes: when a player had an extreme hot stretch, such as a post All-Star run or a strong final 30 games, use the earlier part of his season as the baseline. Elite true shooting over two months usually does not stick. If he had an outlier shooting season on high volume, also expect his attempts to drift back toward his career norm. Before you bid, ask one question: is his value propped up by shooting that may not hold, or does he have room to improve?

sections.heading: Steals and blocks: check the conversion rate

paragraphs.text: Steals are one of the most volatile categories year to year. Do not rely on last season's total. Deflections correlate strongly with steals (0.86), but only 49% of deflections become steals, and luck decides who recovers the ball. Turning deflections into steals repeats at only 0.32. A very high conversion rate is likely to come down.

The swing cuts both ways. Do not pay for a career-high steal rate at the auction. A player whose steals dropped can bounce back, because elite skills like steals tend to return after a down year. A fall from three steals to two cuts a third of his value in that category, and that third can come back. Check his deflections. If they held up while his steals fell, he is a buy.

Blocks are steadier. Turning rim contests into blocks is very sticky (0.82). Shots defended, especially at the rim, correlate with blocks. League average conversion is 13.5%. Expect very high rates to regress. A very low converter could move a couple of points toward average, which adds about 0.2 to 0.3 blocks per game.

Watch for the double hit on blocks. A role or position change can cut his rim contests while his conversion rate also regresses. Elite shot blockers can lose blocks because opponents stop shooting at them. Players who chase blocks also foul more. As players age and their minutes rise, block and foul rates tend to drop, because starters playing big minutes cannot risk foul trouble.

Compare each rate to the player's own career trend, not only to the league. Expect very high numbers to come down and very low numbers to go up. The same logic applies to assists. 58% of potential assists became assists last season. Conversion repeats at only 0.27, and it depends on how well teammates finish. If two teammates both convert poorly, suspect the team before you blame luck.

sections.heading: Where the experts differ on mid-range

paragraphs.text: One view says elite mid-range shooting is rarely repeated year to year. It is low volume, so it swings a lot, and scoring built on tough mid-range shots is a regression risk. The other view says shot quality depends on the player. A contested mid-range shot can be efficient for an elite mid-range shooter and a bad shot for everyone else. In practice, regress a mid-range scorer who had one standout year. Give more trust to one with a long record of making those shots.

sections.heading: In season: three-point swings drive buy-low and sell-high

paragraphs.text: Most buy-low and sell-high calls come from three-point percentage swings. A buy-low player has usually gone cold from three. A sell-high player has shot something like 60% from three early in the season. Because attempts are stable and accuracy is not, check his three-point attempts first. If they hold steady while his percentage sits far from his norm, the gap should close.

Use this in trades with the experienced managers in our league. Sell hot shooters while their 3PTM, PTS and FG% look inflated. Buy cold shooters whose volume and minutes have not changed. Finish these deals before the 2027-03-04 trade deadline so the correction lands in playoff weeks 19 to 21, which end 2027-03-28.

Treat waiver pickups the same way. Hot starts built on numbers that cannot last, like extreme rim finishing, tend to fade. Do not spend big FAB or one of your 6 weekly adds chasing a shooting streak. Spend on role and volume. For defense, look at deflections and rim contests. A player whose steals or blocks lag his deflections or contests is underperforming because of luck and can be added cheaply.
